entities.name: Tobias El Khazen
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tobias El Khazen, born into a prominent Maronite family from Keserwan, assumed the leadership of the Maronite Catholic Church as the 62nd Maronite Patriarch of Antioch, serving from his election in 1756 until his death on May 29, 1766. His tenure, though relatively brief, was marked by significant efforts to consolidate patriarchal authority and navigate the complex political landscape of Ottoman Syria, particularly concerning the internal affairs of the Maronite community and its relationship with both the Ottoman Sublime Porte and the Holy See in Rome. Prior to his patriarchal elevation, El Khazen held the important ecclesiastical posts of Eparch of the Maronite Catholic Archeparchy of Cyprus and later the Maronite Catholic Archeparchy of Tripoli, gaining valuable administrative and pastoral experience that prepared him for the highest office within the Maronite hierarchy.

During his patriarchate, Tobias El Khazen dedicated himself to strengthening the internal discipline of the Maronite Church and affirming its distinct identity amidst the diverse religious communities of the Levant. He focused on administrative reforms, including the management of church properties and the oversight of clerical appointments, aiming to centralize power within the patriarchal see at Bkerké. His period saw continued engagement with Rome, particularly following the Maronite Synod of Mount Lebanon in 1736, whose decrees sought to align Maronite practices more closely with Latin Catholicism. El Khazen's leadership was crucial in implementing these reforms and maintaining the delicate balance between preserving Maronite traditions and fostering closer communion with the Papacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tobias El Khazen's patriarchate was regionally significant for consolidating the Maronite Church's administrative structure and strengthening its ties with Rome during a critical period of Ottoman rule, influencing the future trajectory of Maronite identity and governance.
